question: Compare standard deviation and standard error.
answer: Standard deviation describes the spread of individual observations in a dataset, as per [S1] and [S6]. On the other hand, the standard error quantifies the spread of a statistic, like the sample mean, across different samples, as stated in [S2] and [S6]. also clarifies that standard error is not the same as the variance of the data itself [S6]. further explains that the standard error of the mean is the standard deviation of the sample mean divided by the square root of the sample size [S6]. provides an example where a sample size of 36 results in a standard error of 0.5, while a sample size of 144 halves this to 0.25, making the interval narrower [S6] [S7].

citations.title: Statistics Estimators And Bias
citations.text:
2. Variance of an Estimator
The variance of an estimator describes how much the estimate changes from one random sample
to the next. For the sample mean it equals sigma squared divided by n, so the standard error of the
mean is sigma divided by the square root of n.
This is not the same quantity as the variance of the data themselves, which describes the spread
of individual observations around their mean. Quadrupling the sample size halves the standard
error but does not change the variance of the data.

citations.title: Statistics Confusable Terms
citations.text: standard deviation vs standard error: the standard deviation describes the spread of individual observations; the standard error describes the spread of a statistic such as the sample mean across repeated samples. confidence level vs confidence interval: the level (for example 95%) is a property of the procedure; the interval is the computed range of values. significance level vs p-value: alpha is chosen before the test; the p-value is computed from the data. covariance vs correlation: covariance carries the units of x times the units of y; correlation is unitless and always between -1 and 1. precision of a measurement: how close repeated measurements are to each other. Precision in classification is a different concept (see the machine learning course). normal: the normal distribution is the bell curve. It does not mean "typical" or "healthy" values.

citations.title: Statistics Exercise Guide
citations.text:
Problem 3: Confidence Interval for a Mean
Question. A sample of n = 36 students has mean study time 12.4 hours per week. The population standard deviation is known to be 3 hours. Build a 95% confidence interval.
Solution. The standard error is 3 / sqrt(36) = 0.5. The margin of error is 1.96 * 0.5 = 0.98. The interval is 12.4 plus or minus 0.98, that is (11.42, 13.38). Interpretation: the procedure captures the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples. If the sample size were four times larger (n = 144) the standard error would halve to 0.25 and the interval would become narrower.

S3.title: Statistics Reference Notes
S3.text:
DESCRIPTIVE FORMULAS
Mean: x-bar = (sum of x) / n
Population variance: sigma^2 = sum((x - mu)^2) / N
Sample variance: s^2 = sum((x - x-bar)^2) / (n - 1)
Standard deviation: the square root of the variance.
IQR = Q3 - Q1. Outlier fences: Q1 - 1.5*IQR and Q3 + 1.5*IQR.
Coefficient of variation: CV = standard deviation / mean.

S4.title: Statistics Exercise Guide
S4.text:
Problem 1: Sample versus Population Variance
Question. For the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 compute the population variance and the sample variance.
Solution. The mean is 40 / 8 = 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 32. The population variance is 32 / 8 = 4 and the population standard deviation is 2. Treated as a sample, the sample variance is 32 / 7, about 4.571, and the sample standard deviation is about 2.138. The sample version is larger because it divides by n - 1 instead of n.

S5.title: Statistics Lecture Notes
S5.text: 1. Descriptive Statistics Descriptive statistics summarize a dataset. Measures of central tendency are the mean (the sum of the values divided by the number of values), the median (the middle value of the sorted data) and the mode (the most frequent value). The mean is sensitive to outliers; the median is robust to them. For right-skewed data such as incomes the mean is usually larger than the median. Measures of spread describe variability. The range is maximum minus minimum. The variance averages squared deviations from the mean, and the standard deviation is the square root of the variance, so it has the same units as the data. The interquartile range (IQR) is Q3 minus Q1 and is used to flag outliers: a common rule marks values below Q1 - 1.5 * IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 * IQR. S8.title: Statistics Reference Notes
S8.text:
DISTRIBUTIONS
Binomial: P(X = k) = C(n, k) * p^k * (1 - p)^(n - k)
Poisson: P(X = k) = e^(-lambda) * lambda^k / k!
Normal z-score: z = (x - mu) / sigma
Empirical rule: 68% within 1 sigma, 95% within 2 sigma, 99.7% within 3 sigma.
Standard error of the mean: SE = sigma / sqrt(n)

S9.title: Statistics Lecture Notes
S9.text: 4. Sampling and Confidence Intervals A population is the entire group of interest and a sample is a subset used to learn about it. Simple random sampling gives every member an equal chance of selection; stratified sampling samples within subgroups; convenience sampling is easy but prone to bias. Sampling bias occurs when the sample systematically differs from the population. The sampling distribution of the mean describes how sample means vary from sample to sample. The Central Limit Theorem states that for sufficiently large n the distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal with mean mu and standard error sigma / sqrt(n), regardless of the shape of the original population.
